_comment: The report's cumulative section, one entry per aggregate. Each entry names the tree it describes, so a figure that has fallen behind the branch says so in the rendered table instead of relying on someone remembering. `file` is a perf/scripts/compare_screen.py output under perf/baselines/; `figures` is for an aggregate that is not screen output.
_stock_comment: The commit the stock arm of every aggregate here was measured against. verify_report.py asserts the ref still resolves to it: if next moves, the figures describe a tree that no longer exists and want re-measuring, which should fail a check rather than be noticed by someone eventually.

aggregates.label: Read loop, 57 scenarios
aggregates.note: median of three alternating rounds per arm on one host, both arms proved distinct by content hash before every arm -- stock `74f4a39e7dfc3fbc`, branch `368a99a0401538e6` -- and each hash reproduced exactly on every arm of every round, which is what the fix in finding 80 bought. Query counts were bit-identical across all three rounds on both arms, read from the per-round files rather than from the median, which carries only round 1's booleans: zero unstable in all six runs. Wall-clock spread across rounds is 0.26% on stock and 0.73% on branch, comfortably inside the effect, so the 2-1 ordering lead did not carry it. The scenario set is hand-picked and largely the set this branch optimised, so it describes these pages fairly rather than predicting an arbitrary one; the read screen row is the unbiased check. **This is the first measurement against `next` at `c3605ae48`**, 98 commits on from the `ce01a0464` every earlier figure was taken against, and the stock arm reproduced the old stock arm to the integer on queries and to 0.2% on wall clock, so upstream moved neither

aggregates.label: Read screen, every REST read endpoint
aggregates.note: median of three alternating rounds per arm, enumerated from the URL resolver at run time rather than from a scenario list. **This row exists to check whether the read loop's gain generalises**, because the loop's scenarios are largely the ones this branch optimised. It does. It is REST-only and in-process, so it speaks for neither the UI nor what a user waits for. **The measurements worse on query count are finding 62 working as recorded**: at `?depth=0` a DRF RelatedField never reads the joined columns, so the optimizer prefetches each relation instead of joining it, and queries rise by one per relation while row width collapses -- that finding's own note says the query counter reads it as a regression and must not be the gate. What it buys shows up in the other two columns. **Coverage caveat:** 70 of the 166 endpoints return no rows, so this is breadth over a dataset that does not populate everything, and an empty endpoint measures its fixed cost without being able to show a per-row defect. Stock reproduced the previously recorded stock arm exactly at 15,035 queries

aggregates.label: Write screen, every POST endpoint
aggregates.note: median of three alternating rounds per arm, matched on `(id, kind)` rather than id alone -- the three kinds make 257 measurements from 105 endpoints, and keying on id collapses them to 105. The write path is where query count and wall clock come apart: the wins are Python rather than SQL, so ranking on queries alone undervalues them. **The floor caveat stands, bounded rather than retired** (finding 47): each POST is measured with a minimal schema-valid payload, and across 73 models measured both ways the median understatement is 1.00x, mean 1.31x, max 4.96x -- but 27 models could not be measured with populated payloads at all, including `dcim.cable` and `dcim.interface`, a model with expensive optional relations being both the most understated and the hardest to build a payload for. Stock reproduced the previously recorded stock arm exactly at 22,578 queries

aggregates.coverage: 11,572 objects across 68 models, row counts identical on all four arms
aggregates.label: Whole-workflow apply, 11,572 objects
aggregates.note: four arms in a genuine stock/branch/branch/stock alternation, each from a database reset to the same empty template, the client driven from albert so it cannot compete with the stack it is measuring. Every arm created exactly 11,572 objects and ended with identical row counts -- 536 devices, 1,616 interfaces, 1,648 cables -- with `rc=0` throughout, so the arms provably did the same work. **Of the 785 seconds saved, 7.3 are database execution.** Figures are the mean of two arms per side; within-side agreement runs 0.15% to 1.19% on stock and 0.05% to 1.11% on branch. Arms proved distinct by content hash, stock `74f4a39e7dfc3fbc` against branch `368a99a0401538e6`. The apply is a REST client driving writes with no chrome rendered, so a finding that only touches page chrome cannot appear here. The restore that followed returned the dataset to `2902 8925 3278 2937`, matching `expected-counts.txt`. **Measured against `next` at `c3605ae48`**, where the stock arm landed within 0.2% on wall, 0.6% on queries and 0.3% on database time of the arm previously recorded against `ce01a0464`
